newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts regulators approve NEES plan.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts regulators approve NEES plan.

text.p: Massachusetts Electric Co said its plan to restructure the utility industry and allow customers to choose their electricity supplier beginning January 1, 1998, has been approved by the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities.
The New England Electric System subsidiary is the state's largest retail electric company.
Its plan, called Consumers First, is in the form of a settlement with Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger, the Massachusetts Division of Energy Resources and 14 other parties.

According to its order issued Wednesday, the department found Consumers First "a just and reasonable resolution of restructuring issues for the Company and its ratepayers, and thus...in the public interest."

Consumers First becomes the nation's first negotiated settlement of its kind to receive state approval, the utility said. The plan puts Massachusetts on a faster track to customer choice than most other states which have taken similar action.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission also must accept the plan, which was filed with the FERC on December 3.

"Consumers First demonstrates that a negotiated solution with broad-based support from such groups as consumers, independent power producers, and environmentalists is possible," said NEES chief executive John W. Rowe.
"We now look forward to working with the Legislature as it moves to enact restructuring legislation."
As part of the settlement, Massachusetts Electric affiliate New England Power agreed to sell its electric generation business.

Also, Massachusetts Electric will be allowed to continue to recover the costs of prior commitments through a $0.028 per-kilowatt-hour competitive transition charge. The charge, which is less than the current $0.034, will decline over time, the utility said.

Consumers First requires that Massachusetts Electric continue to deliver to customers electricity and services, including billing, metering, and repairs. However, consumers will purchase their energy supply from one of many competing companies.

For the first seven years of competition, consumers who do not choose a new supplier will have a guaranteed 10 percent savings off their total bill under the plan's "Standard Offer." Consumers who go to the market and choose a supplier may realize even more savings.
Consumers First also has protections for low-income customers, for the environment, and for employees and communities affected by the generation sale.
